opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is pretty simple. When we started working on Toolformer, the observation was that language models are amazing at a lot of things, but they're surprisingly bad at some very basic stuff: arithmetic, knowing what today's date is, looking up a fact they've never seen. And humans are the same, right? We're not great at multiplying big numbers in our heads, so we use a calculator. Tools are a way to extend what the model can do without having to cram everything into the weights.

Where it gets really exciting for synthetic data is this. Post-training is fundamentally bottlenecked by the quality of the signal you give the model. Human annotation is expensive and slow, and honestly, at some point it hits a ceiling. When the model gets good enough, the annotator can't always tell which of two answers is better, especially on hard reasoning or coding. So you need a source of signal that can scale past human ability.

Tools give you grounding. If the model writes code, you can execute it and see whether it runs and whether the tests pass. If it does math, you can check it with a calculator or a solver. If it makes a factual claim, you can check it against search. Suddenly you're not just sampling text from the model and hoping it's correct. You have a verifier in the loop, so you can generate huge amounts of data, filter it with something objective, and train on the good stuff. That loop of generating, verifying, and training is where I think a lot of the progress comes from.

There's also a nice self-supervised aspect, which was the spirit of Toolformer. The model can figure out for itself when a tool call actually helps. You let it try calling an API, see whether the result reduces its uncertainty about what comes next, and keep only the cases where it did. You don't need humans to label "use the calculator here." The model discovers it.

And then looking forward, this is the path to agents. If you want models that can take actions, browse, write and run code, and do multi-step tasks, you need training data of that behavior, and it barely exists on the internet. You kind of have to synthesize it. Tool-augmented models generating their own trajectories, with the environment telling you what worked, is basically the only scalable way I see to get there. So for me it's not a side trick. It's becoming central to how we'll do post-training going forward.

r001.rationale: It says tools extend what a model can do beyond its weights, then describes generating and verifying data and training on the verified examples.

r002.rationale: It lists model weaknesses such as arithmetic and factual lookup, but does not identify targeting those weaknesses as the guiding principle for expert-directed synthetic-data generation.

fable-5.1.text:
So, honestly, I think this is one of the most important things happening in the field right now, and it's the direction I've bet most of my energy on.

Let me step back a bit. When we did Llama 2, and then even more with Llama 3, the thing that became very clear is that for post-training, the quality of the data matters way more than the quantity. And human annotation, which is what everyone started with, has a ceiling. Humans are slow, they're expensive, they're inconsistent, and the thing people don't talk about enough is that humans are often not that good at the task. If you ask a human to write the perfect answer to a hard coding question or a math problem, most annotators will produce something that is actually worse than what the model can already produce. So at some point you cross this line where the model becomes better than your annotators at writing, and then human-written SFT data starts to hurt you more than help you.

So the natural answer is: let the model generate the data. But then you hit the obvious problem, which is, if the model generates its own training data, where does the new signal come from? You're just distilling the model into itself. You can get some gains from rejection sampling, from picking the best of N, but fundamentally you're bounded by what the model already knows.

And this is where tools change everything for me. Because a tool gives you ground truth. If the model writes code and you execute it, you know if it ran, you know if the unit tests passed. If the model does a calculation with a calculator or a Python interpreter, you know the number is correct. If it queries a search engine, it grounds the answer in a real document. So the tool is this external verifier that injects information into the loop that the model did not have in its weights. That's the key thing: you break the circularity. The synthetic data is no longer just the model's prior, it's the model's prior plus a correction from the world.

And once you have a verifier, you can scale this enormously. You can generate millions of problems, millions of attempts, filter with execution, and keep the ones that are actually correct. Nobody has to annotate anything. We did a lot of this for code in Llama 3, with execution feedback, with generating unit tests, and we saw real gains, especially on the long tail of languages and tasks where you would never get enough human data.

The other reason I'm excited, and this is maybe the more speculative part, is that it starts to look like a path toward the model improving itself in a meaningful way. Not in some sci-fi sense, but very concretely: the model proposes tasks, the model solves them, the tools tell you which solutions are right, and you train on that. Each iteration the model gets a bit better, which means it can solve slightly harder problems, which gives you slightly harder data. That's a flywheel. And the reason it works is precisely because of the tools, because they anchor the whole thing to reality.

The limits are real too. It works beautifully where you have a verifier, so code, math, anything with an execution environment. For things like writing a good essay or being helpful in a conversation, you don't have a tool that tells you "yes, this is correct," and there you still need humans or reward models, with all their problems. So I don't think it solves everything. But for a big chunk of what we care about, I think tool-augmented synthetic data is the thing that lets us keep scaling post-training after we've exhausted what humans can give us.

r001.rationale: It says tools provide ground truth that injects information absent from the model’s weights, breaking self-distillation’s circularity.

r002.rationale: It discusses generating harder problems and covering long-tail tasks, but does not identify targeting the model’s specific weaknesses as the guiding principle of expert-directed data generation.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that you can use tools to turn generation into a feedback loop. If a model writes code, it can run it, inspect the error, and try again. You’re no longer relying only on the model’s judgment that its answer looks good—you have feedback from execution.

That makes synthetic data much more interesting for post-training. You can generate tasks, attempt solutions, check the results, and select successful trajectories. And those trajectories can teach more than the final answer: when to call a tool, how to interpret its output, and how to recover from a mistake.

The caveat is that generating more data doesn’t automatically mean generating better data. You need useful tasks and reliable checks. But where you have those, you have a way to scale practice with feedback, and that’s a very exciting direction.

r001.rationale: The response says tool-use trajectories can teach skills such as interpreting outputs and recovering from mistakes, but it does not state that these skills go beyond what is encoded in the model’s weights.

r002.rationale: The response mentions choosing useful tasks and reliable checks, but does not identify targeting the model’s specific weaknesses as the guiding principle for expert-directed generation.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that tools give you a way to ground synthetic data in something beyond the model’s own predictions. If you ask a model to generate an answer and then judge that answer, it can reinforce its own mistakes. But if it can write code, execute it, and inspect the result, you have a much stronger signal about whether it actually solved the problem.

And you can capture the whole process: the first attempt, the tool feedback, the correction. That’s valuable post-training data because you’re teaching the model how to make progress, not just what a polished final answer looks like.

The interesting loop is that a model with tools and more time can solve problems that the same model couldn’t solve in a single response. You can then train on those successful trajectories. It doesn’t make verification or data quality automatic, but it gives you a way to turn additional computation into better training examples.

r001.rationale: The response says tools and extra computation can help a model solve problems it could not solve in one response, but it does not clearly state that training can teach knowledge or skills beyond those encoded in the model’s weights.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify targeting a model’s specific weaknesses as the guiding principle for expert-directed synthetic-data generation.
